Abdominal Mass in a Young Child

organ of origin · age · Wilms tumor vs neuroblastoma · cystic newborn masses · ultrasound, then computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)Where does the mass arise, and how old is the child?

Source vignette Pt – 3 yo F at a well-child visit, normal development and immunizations; BP 156/96; mild right upper and lower quadrant tenderness with a palpable right-sided abdominal mass · Imaging – ultrasound shows a 12-cm heterogeneous solitary mass arising within the upper pole of the right kidney · Q – the most likely diagnosis; options spanned Wilms tumor, neuroblastoma, pheochromocytoma, polycystic kidney disease and renal cell carcinoma

1Presentation
Bottom line
  • Ask two questions of any solid mass: which organ it arises from, and how old the child is
  • Within the kidney at 2 to 5, smooth and not crossing the midline: Wilms tumor; adrenal or sympathetic chain, irregular, crossing the midline, usually under 2: neuroblastoma
  • Ultrasound first; a solid kidney mass usually goes to excision rather than a needle biopsy
What it is

A palpable abdominal mass in an infant or young child, most often painless

Sort by

Organ of origin: kidney, adrenal or sympathetic chain, liver age: cystic masses in the newborn, solid tumors in the toddler

Hands off

Syndromes that need tumor screening: Inherited Tumor Syndromes; hydronephrosis by level: Posterior Urethral Valves

2Urgent risks
NeuroblastomaLeg weakness or new bladder or bowel change: tumor in the spinal canal

If a child with a mass has new weakness, choose MRI of the spine, as for any cord compression.

Wilms tumorA needle biopsy can spill tumor into the peritoneum and raise the stage

If the solid mass arises within the kidney, choose image, then excise; no percutaneous biopsy.

3Differential
Abdominal mass look-alikes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma)Well child; smooth, unilateral flank mass; high blood pressure, hematuria; WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann Denys-Drash syndromeWilms tumor with early-onset nephrotic syndrome from diffuse mesangial sclerosis, and gonadal dysgenesis in a genetic boy (a WT1 mutation). Why the pressure is highWilms tumor raises it through renin or by compressing the renal vessels. Neuroblastoma can raise it through catecholamines, though rarely severely, because it seldom secretes epinephrine.Age 2 to 5; arises within the kidney; does not cross the midline
NeuroblastomaOften an ill child: bone pain, fever, weight loss; periorbital ecchymoses (raccoon eyes), opsoclonus-myoclonus; calcificationsUsually under 2 (median 18 months); adrenal or sympathetic chain, displaces the kidney, may cross the midline; urine vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) and homovanillic acid (HVA) raised
PheochromocytomaEpisodes of headache, sweating and palpitations with high blood pressure; often syndromic
Older child or adult; adrenal, sits on the kidney; metanephrines raised
HepatoblastomaRight upper quadrant mass; Beckwith-WiedemannInfant or toddler; arises in the liver; alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) raised
Hydronephrosis or multicystic dysplastic kidneyThe commonest newborn abdominal masses; fluid-filled on ultrasound
Newborn or infant; a dilated collecting system; or cysts that do not connect, with no working kidney tissue (usually one side, not inherited)
Polycystic kidney diseaseBoth kidneys enlarged and cysticRecessive form in newborns: large echogenic kidneys, hepatic fibrosis, portal hypertension; dominant form in adults
Renal vein thrombosisA stressed newborn: diabetic mother, birth asphyxia, dehydration or polycythemiaNewborn; enlarged kidney with hematuria and thrombocytopenia
Renal cell carcinomaFlank pain, hematuria and a mass; von Hippel-Lindau presents earlierAdult
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Hemihypertrophy, macroglossia, omphalocele, low glucoseBeckwith-Wiedemann: Wilms tumor more often than hepatoblastomaUS every 3 months to age 8; AFP every 3 months to age 4
Aniridia, genitourinary anomaliesWAGR (WT1 deletion); Wilms tumor more often on both sidesUS every 3 months in early childhood
High blood pressure with the massWilms tumor or neuroblastomaThe organ of origin on ultrasound decides

Pause point. The bait: CT or a needle biopsy before ultrasound, or AFP for a kidney mass. Ultrasound shows the organ of origin, and the organ picks the next test.

Practice
  1. 3 yo F at a well-child visit, BP 156/96, palpable right abdominal mass; ultrasound shows a 12-cm heterogeneous solid mass arising within the upper pole of the right kidney → Wilms tumor → excision with chemotherapy, with or without radiation
  2. 14 mo M, irritable for weeks, with rapid chaotic eye movements, jerking of the limbs, and a firm irregular abdominal mass crossing the midline; ultrasound shows calcifications → Neuroblastoma → urine VMA and HVA
  3. 18 mo M with weight loss, bruising around both eyes and a firm left upper quadrant mass lying above the kidney on ultrasound → Urine VMA and HVA → neuroblastoma
  4. 2 yo F, well, whose mother felt a firm painless mass in her left flank while bathing her; BP 118/76, mass smooth and does not cross the midline → Abdominal ultrasound → suspected Wilms tumor
  5. 3-day-old boy with a smooth left flank mass; ultrasound shows multiple noncommunicating cysts of varying size replacing the left kidney with no normal parenchyma, right kidney normal → Multicystic dysplastic kidney → nonfunctioning kidney; the other kidney must be checked
  6. 15 yo F with episodes of pounding headache, sweating and palpitations, BP 172/104 during an episode, and a 4-cm mass above the left kidney → Pheochromocytoma → plasma free metanephrines
  7. 6 mo F with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, 1 week of intermittent vomiting and fussiness, macroglossia, right-sided hemihypertrophy and a firm right upper quadrant mass; serum alpha-fetoprotein 15,678 ng/mL, urine homovanillic and vanillylmandelic acid normal → Hepatoblastoma → liver mass with a very high alpha-fetoprotein
  8. 3 yo M with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome; a screening ultrasound shows a 7-cm solid mass arising within the left kidney; serum alpha-fetoprotein and urine catecholamine metabolites are normal → Wilms tumor → kidney origin with a normal alpha-fetoprotein
  9. 9 mo F, fussy, with a firm right upper quadrant mass that ultrasound places within the right lobe of the liver; the kidneys and adrenals are normal → Serum alpha-fetoprotein → hepatoblastoma
  10. Male newborn at 38 weeks after an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, Apgar scores 8 and 9, normal examination except bilateral flank masses; hematocrit 50%, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, urine with moderate blood and trace protein; ultrasound shows both kidneys enlarged with mixed echogenicity → Polycystic kidney disease → the recessive form; look for hepatic fibrosis
  11. 2-day-old boy whose mother has poorly controlled diabetes, with a new right flank mass, gross hematuria and a platelet count of 70,000/mm3; ultrasound shows one enlarged kidney and a normal left kidney → Renal vein thrombosis → confirm with Doppler ultrasound of the renal vein
Management, in one line Wilms tumor is treated with excision plus chemotherapy, with or without radiation; about 90% of children survive. Tissue at excision or biopsy makes the diagnosis. Ultrasound, not CT (computed tomography), is the first study.
Pearls Establish the origin before weighing age: a mass within the kidney is Wilms tumor; an adrenal or paraspinal mass is neuroblastoma or pheochromocytoma · Hypertension does not separate the two tumors: Wilms raises renin, neuroblastoma releases catecholamines · A well child with a smooth flank mass favors Wilms; an irritable child with weight loss, bone pain or raccoon eyes favors neuroblastoma · Rapid chaotic eye movements with myoclonic jerks in a toddler is opsoclonus-myoclonus, a paraneoplastic sign of neuroblastoma · Two enlarged kidneys in a well newborn suggest ARPKD (autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease); ultrasound shows large echogenic kidneys · ARPKD comes from PKHD1 mutations and brings congenital hepatic fibrosis and Caroli syndrome · Severe ARPKD in utero causes oligohydramnios and Potter sequence · ADPKD (autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease) is the adult form, with kidney and liver cysts and cerebral aneurysms · A creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL on day 1 mirrors the mother's creatinine and does not prove neonatal kidney failure · Neonatal renal vein thrombosis also gives a flank mass and hematuria, usually with thrombocytopenia, in a stressed infant · Avoid repeated deep palpation of a suspected Wilms tumor, because rupture of the capsule spreads tumor · Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome raises the risk of both Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma, so the syndrome alone cannot pick between them · A firm right upper quadrant mass with a very high AFP (alpha-fetoprotein) in an infant is hepatoblastoma · How NBME framed it: the stem names the syndrome and hides the answer in a lab panel, a very high AFP with normal urine HVA (homovanillic acid) and VMA (vanillylmandelic acid) · A syndrome that carries Wilms risk earns surveillance ultrasounds, covered in Part I Inherited Tumor Syndromes
How NBME framed it For the newborn with two flank masses, the key reads only polycystic kidney disease, and the ultrasound says mixed echogenicity rather than cysts · The options are a mass family sorted by age, three tumors plus one vascular mimic, and the labs plant hematuria and a raised creatinine to fit the decoys
Pairs with Part I Inherited Tumor Syndromes covers WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann and the surveillance that follows. Part II Posterior Urethral Valves covers the neonatal flank mass, where hydronephrosis and multicystic dysplastic kidney come first. Part II Acute Leukemia in a Child shares neuroblastoma through marrow infiltration and periorbital ecchymoses. Part I Maternal Effects in the Newborn covers the day-1 creatinine that reflects the mother's kidneys: is the value the mother's or the baby's? Ask: does the mass arise within the kidney, and is the child older than 2?
Transferable rule For a solid mass in a child, name the organ it arises from before naming the tumor, then use age to decide among the rest. A finding two tumors share, such as hypertension, cannot distinguish them.
Unchecked attributeNeuroblastoma is the famous childhood abdominal tumor, but it arises from the adrenal or sympathetic chain and usually before age 2.
Salient decoyPheochromocytoma matches the hypertension and the upper-pole location, but it is adrenal and episodic.
Unchecked attributePolycystic kidney disease gives bilateral cystic kidneys, not one solid mass.
Unchecked attributeRenal cell carcinoma arises within the kidney too, but in adults.
Salient decoyWilms tumor (nephroblastoma): the best-known Beckwith-Wiedemann tumor, but it is a flank mass within the kidney and does not raise AFP (alpha-fetoprotein).
Test-overrides-findingsNeuroblastoma: age 6 months fits it better than Wilms tumor, but urine HVA (homovanillic acid) and VMA (vanillylmandelic acid) are normal.
Unchecked attributeGerm cell tumor: a yolk sac tumor also raises AFP, but in a young child it presents as a pelvic mass, not a firm upper abdominal one.
True-fact-wrong-slotSpina bifida occulta: a raised AFP goes with open neural tube defects in pregnancy, not the closed form, and it makes no abdominal mass.
Unchecked attributeNephroblastoma (Wilms tumor): it shares the flank mass and hematuria; it is usually unilateral and peaks at ages 2 to 5, and this newborn has two masses.
Salient decoyNeuroblastoma: it is the most common solid tumor of infancy; it arises in the adrenal, displaces the kidney rather than enlarging it, and is rarely bilateral.
Unchecked attributeRenal cell carcinoma: it shares a mass within the kidney and hematuria; it is a tumor of adults and adolescents, not newborns.
Unchecked attributeRenal vein thrombosis: it shares a newborn flank mass, hematuria and an enlarged kidney; this baby has no risk factor, with an uncomplicated delivery, good Apgar scores and a normal hematocrit.
